recorded: 11 April 1950, Columbia 30th Street Studio, New York; LP published 1951
question: How much can a returning phrase change while still sounding like an answer?
intro: An unaccompanied piano line calls into silence; a more animated answer brings supporting chords. Debussy returns to that exchange in varied forms, making the pauses and the differences between successive answers part of the miniature’s shape.

sections.label: A · First call and answer
sections.mNote: an unaccompanied call meets a livelier chord-supported answer

sections.label: A′ · The exchange renewed
sections.mNote: the call-and-answer pattern returns with altered melodic details

sections.label: A″ · A larger answer and close
sections.mNote: another call leads to greater animation, then a quiet conclusion

cues.title: A call without accompaniment
cues.text: At first there is only a single line, with little turns and a pause at the end of its phrase. When chords begin to support the answer, listen for the change from a solitary call to something more rhythmically grounded.
cues.evidence: Viewed Durand score, printed p. 22, opens with a single right-hand line and a fermata, followed by Plus mouvementé and supporting left-hand chords. The report’s first substantial rise is around 0:20, with a change at 0:20. No orchestral instrument is claimed. Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0d/IMSLP252526-PMLP02387-Debussy%2C_Claude-Childrens_Corner_Durand_7188_filter.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Leave room for the silence
cues.text: The animated answers do not run straight into the next call. They slow and settle into very quiet held harmonies. Follow that remaining resonance: the space between phrases helps the next unaccompanied line sound newly exposed.
cues.evidence: Viewed score pp. 22–23 repeatedly places Cédez, quiet held chords and rests between the calls. The report shows a withdrawal around 0:35–0:45 before the stronger 0:50 window. This describes the intervening passage, not an exact release or recorded silence.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A pattern, not a literal repeat
cues.text: Listen across the successive exchanges rather than expecting one tune to repeat unchanged. Debussy varies the calls, but the familiar contrast survives: a free-sounding line, then a more animated answer with chords beneath it.
cues.evidence: The two viewed score pages show three related call-and-answer exchanges, with changed melodic details and recurring Plus mouvementé writing. The report has changes at 0:50 and 1:18 separated by a quieter 1:05–1:15 span. The sections group whole exchanges; they do not assign every small phrase its own boundary.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An answer becomes an ending
cues.text: After the fuller later answer, the dance-like figure returns more quietly. Debussy asks it to be held back while preserving the rhythm. Listen for that balance: the phrase relaxes, but its identity should remain clear until the final sustained harmony.
cues.evidence: Viewed score p. 23 gives Un peu retenu (en conservant le rythme), then Cédez and ppp at the final A-major harmony. The report shows its strongest level around 1:30, a withdrawal at 1:35–1:40, a change at 1:46 and quiet final windows. The timing covers the closing paragraph rather than one marked bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Resonance clears for another solitary call
transitions.how: The first animated answer gives way to held, very soft chords. Debussy then removes the accompaniment so another single-line call can emerge, altered in its melodic detail. The accompanying chords subsequently return beneath the more active answer. The repeated formal gesture is the alternation between exposed line and supported movement, not an exact repetition of every note.
transitions.evidence: Viewed Durand score p. 22, third and fourth systems, supplies the held chords, renewed unaccompanied line and chordal answer. The report’s quiet 0:40–0:45 span precedes a change and higher level around 0:50. The section start is an approximate anchor for the renewed exchange.

transitions.title: The same exchange gains a larger reach
transitions.to: A″ · A larger answer and close
transitions.how: Another quiet held harmony clears the way for a renewed call, this time marked a little stronger. The following answer keeps its familiar dotted figures and triplets but becomes more animated, with denser chords and a growing melodic reach. Debussy subsequently brings that figure back softly for the close. The larger third exchange grows from the established pattern rather than introducing an unrelated episode.
transitions.evidence: Viewed score p. 23 supplies the third call, un poco più forte, Plus mouvementé, Poco animato and the subsequent quiet return of the answer. The report’s strongest change is at 1:18, followed by rising level through 1:25–1:30. This anchors the broad exchange, not its precise first note.

composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
French Symbolist poetry · Russian music · Javanese gamelan · eighteenth-century French keyboard music
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
